newsitem.title: FINLAND: Analysts now to focus on Nokia telecoms.
newsitem.headline: Analysts now to focus on Nokia telecoms.

text.p: Finnish telecoms group Nokia Oy posted Q3 profits in line with expectations on Thursday, mainly due to a strong mobile phones comeback, but analysts said they would keep a close eye on infrastructure sales and not yet upgrade forecasts.

Nokia reported a 2.23 billion markka January-September profit before tax and minorities, down from 3.98 billion in the year-ago period, but squarely in line with analysts' median forecast for a 2.20 billion markka profit.
"The result was very good all the way," said Gunnar Andersson at Svenska Handelsbanken in Stockholm.
Richard Kramer at Goldman Sachs in London was particularly pleased with the upturn in Nokia's mobile phones business, where third-quarter sales rose 58 percent year-on-year.
"It was nice to see them reach that inflection point where mobile phones profitability is coming back to where it was last year," he said.
Analyst Jyrki Hilli at Arctos Securities said: "The mobile phone division's return to such strong growth was a very good piece of news."
Asked what the strong growth in mobile phones sales tells about the market, Stuart Jeffrey at Daiwa in London said: "It tells us that Motorola is not doing so well."
Nokia said mobile phones sales growth was especially strong in Asia and Europe, but Jeffrey did not think this indicated any particular weakness for Nokia in the U.S.

Angela Dean, analyst at Morgan Stanley in London, said she was unlikely to make any major changes in her forecasts nor to her "neutral" recommendation for the stock unless something unexpected came out of a teleconference later on Thursday.
"The figures were pretty much in line with what we were going for," Dean said.
Other analysts also said they would not be making big changes in their Nokia earnings forecasts or to their recommendations for the stock.
"(The nine-month report) will not change our recommendation on Nokia. We already had a positive view, and this does not change that," Handelsbanken's Andersson said.
But analysts will now shift their focus to the telecommunications infrastructure division, where Nokia said third-quarter sales growth of 26 percent had been slower than expected.

In August, Nokia said in the first-half report its telecommunications division's revenues would be weighted toward the second half of the year, but third-quarter sales growth came out slower than the 30 percent recorded in January-June.
Kramer at Goldman Sachs said telecommunications infrastructure sales could become a worry.

"It may be that Nokia still has considerable infrastructure business to come in the fourth quarter, but the current level of growth remains below what the company indicated at the start of the year," he said.
Niklas Geust at FIM Securities, said Q4 growth in the telecommunications division, which after mobile phones is the second largest Nokia division, should preferably be over 35 percent.

But Andersson said the slightly slower than expected pace of growth in telecommunications sales was no real cause for concern, and put it down to seasonal factors. "You have strong seasonal patterns in that area," he said.
Nor did Daiwa's Jeffrey see the slow-down as a problem.
"I don't see it suggesting trouble ... I would put it down to a dip rather than a long-term trend," he said.
--Ilkka Virtanen, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-6805 0248
